Ice Age History for Sleep 🌙 How Did Ancient Humans Sleep?

Premieres Mon 26 Oct at 5 PM ET (21:00 UTC) · About 1 hour 58 min · narrated slowly for sleep

Find it on our YouTube channel

The video goes public on the channel at the premiere time.

How did ancient humans sleep? A bedtime story for grown-ups in calming history narration: relaxing bedtime history from one long Ice Age night.

🌙 No mid-video ads, nothing to wake you.

At least two hundred thousand years ago, in a cave in southern Africa, people were already making beds. Tonight we spend one long Ice Age night about eighteen thousand years ago in an imagined camp of mammoth-bone houses on the cold plains of eastern Europe: dusk on the mammoth steppe, the house of bones, gathering the fire, needles and furs, the oldest grass beds of Border Cave and Sibudu, the nests our ape relatives build each evening, the watcher by the fire, what modern sleep studies of the Hadza, San and Tsimane suggest, "first sleep" and "second sleep", and first light on the steppe.

Along the way we keep a clear line between what archaeology and sleep research actually show, and what we can only imagine. The family, their dog and their words are invented; the world around them is built from real finds.

This is a slow, calm bedtime documentary, narrated softly to help you relax, unwind, and drift off to sleep. There are no loud sounds, no sudden changes and no horror: just a quiet voice, slow images, and a small fire in a house of bones.

About this sleep story

About 1 hour 58 min, narrated slowly for sleep, with no ad breaks. Made as history to fall asleep to: it's fine to drift off partway, and the chapters below let you find your place again.

Nobody wrote anything down in the Ice Age, so this episode tries to show where the evidence stops. The grass beds of Border Cave and Sibudu, the mammoth-bone houses and the sleep studies of the Hadza, San and Tsimane are real; the family, their dog and their stories are imagined. Where researchers disagree, as on early cooking or Roger Ekirch's "first sleep", the narration says so.

Sources

Researched and written for this channel from these sources. Where historians disagree, the narration says so.

  • Wadley et al. (2020), "Fire and grass-bedding construction 200 thousand years ago at Border Cave, South Africa", Science
  • Wadley et al. (2011), "Middle Stone Age bedding construction and settlement patterns at Sibudu, South Africa", Science
  • Samson et al. (2017), "Chronotype variation drives night-time sentinel-like behaviour in hunter–gatherers", Proceedings of the Royal Society B
  • Yetish et al. (2015), "Natural sleep and its seasonal variations in three pre-industrial societies", Current Biology
  • A. Roger Ekirch, At Day's Close: Night in Times Past (2005)
  • Polly Wiessner (2014), "Embers of society: Firelight talk among the Ju/'hoansi Bushmen", PNAS
  • Richard Wrangham, Catching Fire: How Cooking Made Us Human (2009)
  • Research on the mammoth-bone dwellings of Mezhyrich and the Kostenki sites (Quaternary International, Journal of Archaeological Science)
